source: Dionysii Cartusiani Opera Omnia, t. II (Montreuil)

1.title: Expositio litteralis primi capituli libri Exodi: Hæc sunt nomina filiorum Israel
1.title_en: Literal exposition of the first chapter of the book of Exodus: “These are the names of the children of Israel”

paras.t: Moyses in libri hujus exordio continuat historiam nunc exponendam, historiæ libri præcedentis, videlicet Genesis. Circa quod in Scholastica historia ex verbis sancti Hieronymi dicitur: Historia Exodi non est alia ab historia Genesis, sed eadem continuata, quæ propter tollendum fastidium, in quinque partitiones, id est in quinque libros, divisa est. Contra quod objici posset, quod in Exodo multa narrantur, puta decem plagæ, divisio maris Rubri, submersio Ægyptiorum, de quibus in Genesi nihil habetur, et facta sunt diu post ea quæ in Genesi recitantur. Ad quod dici potest, quod dicitur historia eadem, quia de eodem est populo Hebræorum.
paras.en: At the beginning of this book Moses joins the history now to be expounded to the history of the preceding book, namely Genesis. On this the Scholastic History [the biblical history of Peter Comestor, the "Master of the Histories"] says, from the words of St. Jerome: The history of Exodus is not another than the history of Genesis, but the same one continued, which, to avoid weariness, was divided into five portions, that is, into five books. Against this it could be objected that many things are told in Exodus, such as the ten plagues, the dividing of the Red Sea and the drowning of the Egyptians, of which nothing is found in Genesis, and which took place long after the things related in Genesis. To this it can be said that it is called the same history because it is about the same people of the Hebrews.

paras.t: Itaque ait: Hæc sunt nomina filiorum Israel, hoc est ipsius Jacob, qui alio nomine vocatus est Israel, ut dictum est in Genesi, qui ingressi sunt in Ægyptum cum Jacob. Singuli cum domibus suis introierunt, Ruben, Simeon, Levi, Judas, Issachar, Zabulon: istos sex genuit Jacob ex Lia eodem ordine, quo hic exponuntur; et Benjamin, quem genuit ex Rachele; Dan et Nephthali, quos genuit ex Bala ancilla Rachelis; Gad et Aser, quos ex Zelpha famula Liæ genuit, ut in Genesi habitum est. Hi undecim intraverunt cum Jacob Ægyptum, singuli cum domibus suis, id est unusquisque eorum cum sobole sua, sicut in Genesi habetur.
paras.en: So he says: [[1:1|These are the names of the children of Israel|Hæc sunt nomina filiorum Israel]], that is, of Jacob himself, who was called by another name Israel, as was said in Genesis, [[1:1|that went into Egypt with Jacob: they went in every man with his household|qui ingressi sunt in Ægyptum cum Jacob. Singuli cum domibus suis introierunt]]: [[1:2|Ruben, Simeon, Levi, Juda,|Ruben, Simeon, Levi, Judas,]] [[1:3|Issachar, Zabulon|Issachar, Zabulon]]: these six Jacob begot of Lia, in the same order in which they are set out here[[Gen 29:1||]][[Gen 30:1||]]; [[1:3|and Benjamin|et Benjamin]], whom he begot of Rachel; [[1:4|Dan, and Nephthali|Dan et Nephthali]], whom he begot of Bala, the handmaid of Rachel; [[1:4|Gad and Aser|Gad et Aser]], whom he begot of Zelpha, the servant of Lia, as was found in Genesis. These eleven went into Egypt with Jacob, every man with his household, that is, each of them with his offspring, as is found in Genesis.

paras.t: Erant igitur omnes animæ eorum qui egressi sunt de femore Jacob, id est eorum qui secundum carnem nati sunt ex Jacob, septuaginta. Aliqui textus habent, septuaginta quinque. Atque (ut refert Lyra) in Hebræo habetur, septuaginta. In Genesi quoque sic legitur: Omnes animæ domus Jacob, quæ ingressæ sunt in Ægyptum, fuerunt septuaginta. Quæ omnia qualiter verificentur et concordentur, diffuse est introductum in expositione capituli quadragesimi sexti Geneseos. Porro ex Jacob nati sunt immediate solum duodecim filii, et filia una. Quod ergo tam multi, sicut jam tactum est, dicuntur nati ex femore ejus, intelligendum est simul tam de illis quos genuit immediate, quam de nepotibus suis, videlicet filiis filiorum suorum, quos nepotes genuit mediate. Joseph autem in Ægypto erat. Fuit enim et habitavit in Ægypto diu ante ingressum patris sui in eam et diu post obitum ejus. Istud autem cum clausula subsequenti hic interponitur, ad continuandum dictis dicenda.
paras.en: [[1:5|And all the souls that came out of Jacob's thigh|Erant igitur omnes animæ eorum qui egressi sunt de femore Jacob]], that is, of those who were born of Jacob according to the flesh, [[1:5|were seventy|septuaginta]]. Some texts have seventy-five. And (as Lyra reports) the Hebrew has seventy. In Genesis too we read thus: [[Gen 46:27|All the souls of the house of Jacob, that entered into Egypt, were seventy|Omnes animæ domus Jacob, quæ ingressæ sunt in Ægyptum, fuerunt septuaginta]]. How all these things are true and agree has been set out at length in the exposition of the forty-sixth chapter of Genesis. Now of Jacob there were born immediately only twelve sons and one daughter. That so many, then, as has just been touched on, are said to have been born of his thigh[[Gen 46:26||]] [the book of the margin's reference is lost; Gen 46:26 fits] must be understood both of those whom he begot immediately and of his grandsons, namely the sons of his sons, which grandsons he begot mediately. [[1:5|but Joseph was in Egypt|Joseph autem in Ægypto erat]]. For he was and dwelt in Egypt long before his father's coming into it, and long after his death. This, with the clause that follows, is put in here to join what is to be said to what has been said.

paras.t: Nam subditur: Quo mortuo, quum esset centum et decem annorum, et universis fratribus ejus, omnique cognatione illa, id est, omnibus illis, qui cum Jacob introierunt Ægyptum, defunctis, non tamen posteritate illorum, quum subsequatur: filii Israel creverunt per generationem et augmentationem, et quasi germinantes multiplicati sunt, id est, instar seminum in terram projectorum, sive herbarum, aucti sunt numero; ac roborati nimis, impleverunt terram. Nam unusquisque aliquid roboris addidit multitudini suæ plebis.
paras.en: For it goes on: [[1:6|After he was dead|Quo mortuo]], when he was a hundred and ten years old, [[1:6|and all his brethren, and all that generation|et universis fratribus ejus, omnique cognatione illa]], that is, when all those who went into Egypt with Jacob had died, though not their posterity, since there follows: [[1:7|The children of Israel increased|filii Israel creverunt]] by begetting and growth, [[1:7|and sprung up into multitudes|et quasi germinantes multiplicati sunt]], that is, they grew in number like seeds cast into the ground, or like plants; [[1:7|and growing exceedingly strong they filled the land|ac roborati nimis, impleverunt terram]]. For each one added some strength to the multitude of his people.

paras.t: Circa hoc recitat Lyra: Dicunt Hebræi, quod mulieres Hebrææ in quolibet partu pariebant plures pueros sive proles, et aliquando quatuor proles, interdum usque ad sex. Propter quod dicitur, Quasi germinantes: quasi dicatur, Sicut ex uno grano multa grana nascuntur. Huic recitationi satis concordat, quod Rabbi Paulus scribit: Multiplicatio, inquiens, filiorum Israel tanta erat, quod assimilabatur terræ nascentium germinationi, quæ ex paucis granis multum affert fructum. Unde in Ezechiele Dominus loquitur Synagogæ: Multiplicatam quasi germen agri dedi te. Verumtamen istud apparentiam modicam habet, nec naturale fuisset, nec unquam antea legitur factum, nec necesse est dicere. Nam dato quod feminæ non genuerint uno partu nisi unicam prolem aut duas, nihilo minus littera ista verificatur. Nam homines tunc satis diu vixerunt: et mulieres usque ad septuaginta aut octoginta annos fuerunt fecundæ, ita quod eadem uxor poterat successive parere quadraginta proles, aut circiter. Idem quoque vir poterat plures habere uxores, ut patuit. Ex quibus potuit multos gignere pueros, sicut et Gedeon legitur septuaginta filios habuisse.
paras.en: On this Lyra reports: The Hebrews say that the Hebrew women at every birth brought forth several children or offspring, sometimes four, at times as many as six. That is why it says [[1:7|sprung up|Quasi germinantes]] [Latin *quasi germinantes*, "as if sprouting"]: as if to say, as from one grain many grains spring up. With this report agrees well what Rabbi Paul [Paul of Burgos, a converted rabbi who wrote additions to Lyra's Postill] writes: The multiplying of the children of Israel, he says, was so great that it was likened to the sprouting of the things that grow from the earth, which from a few grains bears much fruit. Hence in Ezechiel the Lord says to the Synagogue: [[Ezech 16:7|I caused thee to multiply as the bud of the field|Multiplicatam quasi germen agri dedi te]]. Yet this has little likelihood: it would not have been natural, it is never read to have happened before, and there is no need to say it. For granting that the women bore only one child, or two, at a birth, this text is nonetheless borne out. For men lived quite long then, and women were fruitful up to seventy or eighty years, so that the same wife could bear forty children one after another, or thereabouts. The same man could also have several wives, as has been seen; and from them he could beget many children, as Gedeon too is read to have had seventy sons[[Judg 8:30||]].

paras.t: Surrexit interea rex novus super Ægyptum, qui ignorabat Joseph. In Scholastica fertur historia, quod rex iste fuit octavus ab illo, sub quo Joseph præfuit in Ægypto, nec fuit rex iste de semine regis illius, cujus jam defecit successio. Hinc dilectio, quam posteri illius prioris regis habuerunt ad filios Israel, propter Joseph et beneficia ejus, defuit regi huic: ideo dicitur ignorasse Joseph, quoniam beneficia et historiam Joseph oblitus fuit, vel ob longitudinem temporis non audivit.
paras.en: [[1:8|In the mean time there arose a new king over Egypt, that knew not Joseph|Surrexit interea rex novus super Ægyptum, qui ignorabat Joseph]]. The Scholastic History says that this king was the eighth from the one under whom Joseph was ruler in Egypt, and that this king was not of the seed of that king, whose line had by now died out. Hence the love which the descendants of that earlier king had for the children of Israel, on account of Joseph and his benefits, was wanting in this king. Therefore he is said not to have known Joseph, because he had forgotten the benefits and the history of Joseph, or, by reason of the length of time, had not heard of them.

paras.t: Et ait ad populum suum: Ecce populus filiorum Israel multus, et fortior nobis est. Non est putandum, quod absolute loquendo Israeliticus ille populus in Ægypto degens, fuerit major, fortior aut ditior toto populo Ægyptiorum; sed comparando numerum ad numerum, fortiores fuerunt illi Hebræi Ægyptiis: idcirco si verbum regis verificari debet, oportet ut intelligatur per modum hyperbolicæ locutionis, qua aliquid dicitur per excessum: per quem modum multæ propositiones in Genesi scriptæ sunt, ut quod Pharao dixit ad Joseph, Absque tuo imperio nullus movebit manum aut pedem in tota terra Ægypti. Non tamen oportet hæc verba impii regis illius a mendacio excusare. Ipse namque sic loquebatur, quatenus Ægyptios vehementius inflammaret contra Hebræos. Ex passione quoque invidiæ, quam contra Hebræos concepit, prosperitas eorumdem videbatur ei major quam fuit. Passiones namque, quando non reprimuntur per rationis judicium et virtutes morales, semper abducunt rationem a medio, et ejus pervertunt judicium tanto plus, quanto magis intensæ sunt in se ipsis.
paras.en: [[1:9|And he said to his people: Behold the people of the children of Israel are numerous and stronger than we|Et ait ad populum suum: Ecce populus filiorum Israel multus, et fortior nobis est]]. It is not to be thought that, speaking absolutely, that Israelite people living in Egypt was greater, stronger or richer than the whole people of the Egyptians; but comparing number with number, those Hebrews were stronger than the Egyptians. Therefore, if the king's word is to be true, it must be understood as a hyperbolic way of speaking, in which something is said by excess. In this way many statements were written in Genesis, as what Pharao said to Joseph: [[Gen 41:44|without thy commandment no man shall move hand or foot in all the land of Egypt|Absque tuo imperio nullus movebit manum aut pedem in tota terra Ægypti]]. Yet there is no need to excuse these words of that wicked king from falsehood. For he spoke so in order to inflame the Egyptians more fiercely against the Hebrews. And from the passion of envy that he had conceived against the Hebrews, their prosperity seemed to him greater than it was. For the passions, when they are not held in check by the judgement of reason and by the moral virtues, always draw reason away from the mean, and pervert its judgement the more, the more intense they are in themselves.

paras.t: Venite, sapienter, mihi consentiendo, et ea quæ dixero adimplendo, opprimamus eum. Rex iste iniquus, suam iniquam astutiam reputavit esse veram prudentiam. Habet autem vulpina versutia aliquid simile cum vera prudentia. Nam sicut veraciter prudens honestum sibi finem præfigit, et juxta exigentiam finis illius bene disponit media sua ad finis illius adeptionem: sic astutus et carnaliter prudens, præligit sibi finem perversum, videlicet carnaliter delectari, impie prosperari, aut prævalere, aut aliquid tale, et juxta quod congruit ad obtinendum finem hujusmodi, apte disponit de mediis. Ne forte multiplicetur in sexu virili plus quam multiplicatus est; et si ingruerit contra nos bellum, addatur inimicis nostris: hoc est, ne sponte se addat adversariis nostris, eosque juvet ad expugnandum nos. Ideo subditur: expugnatisque nobis, egrediatur de terra, id est, terram nostram libere exeat in damnum nostrum. Erant namque Hebræi subjecti Ægyptiis, et utiles eis erant in multis, puta in artificiis, atque (ut fertur) dabant regi annuatim magnum tributum. Et forsan rex iste aliquid percepit de spe, quam habuerunt Hebræi de sua liberatione ex Ægypto, et introductione in terram ipsis a Deo suo promissam: ideo videns eos sic multiplicari ac roborari, verebatur ne congregato exercitu per vim exirent.
paras.en: [[1:10|Come let us wisely|Venite, sapienter]], by agreeing with me and carrying out what I shall say, [[1:10|oppress them|opprimamus eum]]. This wicked king thought his wicked cunning to be true prudence. Now foxlike craft has something in common with true prudence. For just as the truly prudent man sets himself a good end, and, as that end requires, rightly orders his means to the gaining of it, so the crafty and carnally prudent man chooses for himself a perverse end, namely carnal pleasure, wicked prosperity, getting the upper hand, or something of the kind, and fitly orders his means as suits the gaining of such an end. [[1:10|lest they multiply|Ne forte multiplicetur]] in the male sex more than they have multiplied already; [[1:10|and if any war shall rise against us, join with our enemies|et si ingruerit contra nos bellum, addatur inimicis nostris]]: that is, lest of their own accord they join our adversaries and help them to defeat us. Therefore it goes on: [[1:10|and having overcome us, depart out of the land|expugnatisque nobis, egrediatur de terra]], that is, go freely out of our land, to our loss. For the Hebrews were subject to the Egyptians and were useful to them in many things, for instance in crafts, and (so it is said) they paid the king a great tribute every year. And perhaps this king had caught something of the hope which the Hebrews had of their deliverance from Egypt and of their being brought into the land promised them by their God. So, seeing them multiply and grow strong in this way, he feared that they would gather an army and go out by force.

paras.t: Præposuit itaque eis magistros operum, ut affligerent eos oneribus. Quidam dicunt quod isti magistri operum fuerunt Ægyptii: quod etiam asserit Lyra. Alii dicunt quod fuerunt Hebræi, et quod ipsis magistris operum præfecit quosdam Ægyptios, qui magistros illos operum Hebræos sollicitarent ad expletionem sui officii. Et hoc asserit Magister in historiis, et consonat Josepho, imo et textui infra, quo legitur: Præcepit Pharao præfectis operum, et exactoribus populi, dicens: Nequaquam ultra dabitis paleas populo. Itemque: Flagellatique sunt qui præerant operibus filiorum Israel, ab exactoribus Pharaonis. Et certum est, quod illi sic flagellati, fuerunt Hebræi. Ideo istud tanquam verum tenendum est. Itaque rex Ægypti præfecit Hebræis magistros operum, ut ipsi magistri operum affligerent Hebræos oneribus, hoc est, ut laboriosa opera eis imponerent ex parte regis, quatenus ipsi Hebræi fatigati et fracti laboribus, tædio ac mœrore, non vacarent amplexibus. Sicque in illis operibus quærebat Pharao propriam utilitatem, et Hebræorum diminutionem, quam et principaliter intendebat.
paras.en: [[1:11|Therefore he set over them masters of the works, to afflict them with burdens|Præposuit itaque eis magistros operum, ut affligerent eos oneribus]]. Some say that these masters of the works were Egyptians, and Lyra also asserts this. Others say that they were Hebrews, and that over these masters of the works he set certain Egyptians, to urge those Hebrew masters of the works to fulfil their office. And this the Master of the Histories asserts, and it agrees with Josephus, and indeed with the text below, where we read: Pharao [[Ex 5:6|commanded|Præcepit]] [[Ex 5:6|the overseers of the works, and the task-masters of the people, saying|præfectis operum, et exactoribus populi, dicens]]: [[Ex 5:7|You shall give straw no more to the people|Nequaquam ultra dabitis paleas populo]]. And again: [[Ex 5:14|they that were over the works of the children of Israel, were scourged by Pharao's taskmasters|Flagellatique sunt qui præerant operibus filiorum Israel, ab exactoribus Pharaonis]]. And it is certain that those who were scourged in this way were Hebrews. Therefore this is to be held as true. So the king of Egypt set masters of the works over the Hebrews, so that these masters of the works should afflict the Hebrews with burdens, that is, lay toilsome works on them on the king's behalf, so that the Hebrews, wearied and broken with labours, weariness and grief, should have no leisure for embraces. And thus in those works Pharao sought his own profit and the lessening of the Hebrews, which was in fact his chief aim.

paras.t: Ædificaveruntque Hebræi urbes tabernaculorum Pharaoni, Phithom et Ramesses, hoc est urbes ita vocatas. Secundum Lyram, in Hebræo habetur, Urbes thesaurorum, quia tam fortes tunc factæ sunt illæ urbes, ac si ibi essent thesauri regis ponendi. Sed potius puto, quod S. Hieronymus transtulit sicut in Hebræo habetur, et quod dictio illa Hebraica, pro qua transtulit, Tabernaculorum, forte æquivoca sit ad designandum tabernacula ac thesauros. Nam et Josephus innuit, in Hebræo haberi, Urbes tabernaculorum.
paras.en: [[1:11|and they built for Pharao cities of tabernacles, Phithom, and Ramesses|Ædificaveruntque Hebræi urbes tabernaculorum Pharaoni, Phithom et Ramesses]], that is, the cities so called. According to Lyra the Hebrew has "cities of treasures", because those cities were then made as strong as if the king's treasures were to be put there. But I rather think that St. Jerome translated as the Hebrew has it, and that the Hebrew word for which he wrote "of tabernacles" is perhaps ambiguous, meaning both tabernacles and treasures. For Josephus too implies that the Hebrew has "cities of tabernacles".

paras.t: Porro in Scholastica fertur historia, quod urbes illæ jam ante fuerunt urbes, sed non urbes tabernaculorum, erantque in extremitate Ægypti: ideo Pharao fecit eas muris vallari, ut poneret in eis armatos quasi in tabernaculis jugiter excubantes, ne ingredi quis posset aut egredi sine regis consensu. Vel dicuntur urbes tabernaculorum, præ multitudine habitaculorum ibi exsistentium, aut propter fortitudinem fortalitiorum ibidem factorum, in quibus milites regis erant; sive ut aliqui dicunt, tabernaculorum, id est positionum, ubi videlicet fiscus regis reponeretur.
paras.en: Further, the Scholastic History says that those cities were cities already before, but not cities of tabernacles, and they lay at the border of Egypt. So Pharao had them walled round, to put armed men in them keeping watch continually as in tents, so that no one could go in or out without the king's consent. Or they are called cities of tabernacles because of the great number of dwellings there, or because of the strength of the fortresses built there, in which the king's soldiers were; or, as some say, "of tabernacles", that is, of storehouses [Latin *positionum*, "places of putting away"], where the king's treasury was to be laid up.

paras.t: Porro Pharao est nomen commune regiæ dignitatis regum Ægypti, sicut apud Romanos quilibet imperator dicebatur Augustus. Ideo Rabanus in libro de Naturis rerum: Pharao, inquit, est nomen non hominis, sed honoris. Et Glossa: Omnes reges Ægyptiorum, Pharaones vocabantur, sicut et postea Ptolemæi vocati sunt; et reges Persarum, Arsacidæ; reges vero Romanorum, dicti sunt Cæsares vel Augusti, et præter hæc habuerunt propria nomina.
paras.en: Further, Pharao is a name common to the royal dignity of the kings of Egypt, as among the Romans every emperor was called Augustus. Hence Rabanus in the book On the Natures of Things: Pharao, he says, is the name not of a man but of an honour. And the Gloss: All the kings of the Egyptians were called Pharaos, as afterwards they were called Ptolemies; and the kings of the Persians, Arsacids; while the rulers of the Romans were called Caesars or Augusti; and besides these they had their own names.

paras.t: Quantoque opprimebant eos, tanto magis multiplicabantur et crescebant, hoc est, quanto plus Hebræi opprimebantur ab Ægyptiis per labores, tanto Hebræi genuerunt sobolem abundantiorem. Quod quidam adscribunt miraculo. Unde et Rabbi Paulus dicit hoc non fuisse secundum naturalem communemque cursum. Alii dicunt, quod experientia docet, rusticanos et graviter laborantes gignere prolem copiosiorem quam eos qui laute vivunt et otio vacant.
paras.en: [[1:12|But the more they oppressed them, the more they were multiplied and increased|Quantoque opprimebant eos, tanto magis multiplicabantur et crescebant]], that is, the more the Hebrews were oppressed by the Egyptians with labours, the more abundant the offspring the Hebrews begot. Some put this down to a miracle; hence Rabbi Paul too says that this was not according to the natural and common course. Others say that experience teaches that country people and those who labour hard beget more plentiful offspring than those who live in comfort and give themselves to leisure.

paras.t: Oderantque [filios] Israel Ægyptii. Josephus breviter tangit quatuor causas odii hujus, dicens: Oderunt Hebræos Ægyptii propter virtutem ingenii, et laboris industriam, et affluentiam opum, et sobolis nobilitatem. Primo itaque oderant eos, quia Hebræi erant eis ingeniosiores. Secundo, quoniam erant eis in artificiis subtiliores. Tertio, quoniam divites erant et ditiores vulgo Ægyptiorum. Quarto, quoniam elegantem et copiosam sobolem habuerunt. In Genesi quoque præhabitum est, quod Ægyptii abominabantur Hebræos propter disparem cultum, et tanquam alienos spreverunt eos. Et affligebant Ægyptii Hebræos, illudentes et invidentes eis, verbis, signis, et factis: atque ad amaritudinem perducebant vitam eorum operibus duris luti et lateris, omnique famulatu, quo in terræ operibus premebantur, hoc est per opera inhumaniter laboriosa, quæ materialiter fiebant ex terra lutosa atque lateribus, ex quibus ædificabant urbes tabernaculorum. Denique in Scholastica historia ex Josepho dicitur: Aliud opus non tam grave, quam servile, imposuit Pharao eis, ut scilicet lutum platearum et sordes vicorum cophinis exportarent, juxta illud in Psalmo, Manus ejus in cophinis servierunt: atque ut fluvium, scilicet Nilum, per multas derivationes dividerent, quatenus terram Ægypti in locis plurimis irrigaret, et circumdarent civitates fossatis, ne eas fluvius inundaret.
paras.en: [[1:13|And the Egyptians hated the children of Israel|Oderantque [filios] Israel Ægyptii]]. Josephus briefly touches on four causes of this hatred, saying: The Egyptians hated the Hebrews for their power of mind, their diligence in labour, their abundance of wealth, and the excellence of their offspring. First, then, they hated them because the Hebrews were cleverer than they; secondly, because they were more skilful than they in crafts; thirdly, because they were rich, and richer than the common people of the Egyptians; fourthly, because they had fine and plentiful offspring. It was also said earlier in Genesis that the Egyptians held the Hebrews in abomination because of their different worship[[Gen 46:34||]] [the margin's chapter is lost; Gen 46:34, where the Egyptians abhor shepherds, fits], and despised them as foreigners. [[1:13|and afflicted them|Et affligebant Ægyptii Hebræos]], [[1:13|and mocked them|illudentes]] and envied them, in words, signs and deeds: [[1:14|And they made their life bitter with hard works in clay and brick, and with all manner of service, wherewith they were overcharged in the works of the earth|atque ad amaritudinem perducebant vitam eorum operibus duris luti et lateris, omnique famulatu, quo in terræ operibus premebantur]], that is, with inhumanly toilsome works, made materially of muddy earth and bricks, from which they built the cities of tabernacles. Lastly, the Scholastic History says, from Josephus: Pharao laid on them another work, not so heavy as servile, namely that they should carry out in baskets the mud of the streets and the filth of the lanes, according to that word in the Psalm: [[Ps 80:7|his hands had served in baskets|Manus ejus in cophinis servierunt]]; and that they should divide the river, that is, the Nile, by many channels, so that it might water the land of Egypt in a great many places, and surround the cities with ditches, so that the river should not flood them.

paras.t: Dixit autem rex Ægypti obstetricibus Hebræorum, quarum una vocabatur Sephora, altera Phua. Pharao videns sibi non prodesse præinductam versutiam ad minorandum populum Hebræorum, excogitavit alium dolum, ut scilicet obstetrices Hebræorum obstetricando occiderent masculos Hebræorum, ut patet in textu. Porro hæ duæ obstetrices præerant ceteris obstetricibus Hebræorum, quibus duæ obstetrices nequaquam sufficiebant. Itaque his duabus, et per eas ceteris Hebræorum obstetricibus jussit, præcipiens eis: Quando obstetricabitis Hebræas, et tempus partus advenerit, si masculus fuerit, interficite eum. Atque, ut Magister in historiis addit, permisit eis ut mentirentur factum esse abortum. Primo namque volebat rex propositum suum per fraudes occulte implere, ne de nimia crudelitate argueretur.
paras.en: [[1:15|And the king of Egypt spoke to the midwives of the Hebrews: of whom one was called Sephora, the other Phua|Dixit autem rex Ægypti obstetricibus Hebræorum, quarum una vocabatur Sephora, altera Phua]]. Pharao, seeing that the craft he had used before did not help him to lessen the people of the Hebrews, devised another trick, namely that the midwives of the Hebrews should kill the Hebrews' males while delivering them, as is plain in the text. Now these two midwives were over the other midwives of the Hebrews, for whom two midwives would by no means have been enough. So he gave his order to these two, and through them to the other midwives of the Hebrews, [[1:16|Commanding them: When you shall do the office of midwives to the Hebrew women, and the time of delivery is come: if it be a man child, kill it|præcipiens eis: Quando obstetricabitis Hebræas, et tempus partus advenerit, si masculus fuerit, interficite eum]]. And, as the Master of the Histories adds, he allowed them to lie that a miscarriage had taken place. For at first the king wished to carry out his purpose secretly by frauds, so as not to be charged with excessive cruelty.

paras.t: Si femina, reservate, hoc est, si proles nata fuerit femella, vivere eam permittite. Ægyptii quippe non timuerunt sibi imminere periculum ex multiplicatione feminarum Hebræarum, quia infirmus, non bellicosus, est sexus femineus: ideo quoque voluerunt eas servari, ut earum fruerentur concubitu. Est et tertia causa, cur rex præcepit feminas reservari: quia videlicet feminæ Hebræ in quibusdam artificiis erant subtiliores mulieribus Ægyptiorum; ideo rex voluit, ut in talibus artificiis sibi ac populo suo servirent, et ut possideret eas in ancillas.
paras.en: [[1:16|if a woman, keep it alive|Si femina, reservate]], that is, if the child born is a girl, let her live. For the Egyptians did not fear that any danger threatened them from the multiplying of the Hebrew women, because the female sex is weak and not warlike; and for this reason too they wished them to be kept, so as to enjoy their bed. There is also a third reason why the king commanded the females to be kept: namely, because the Hebrew women were more skilful in certain crafts than the women of the Egyptians; so the king wished them to serve him and his people in such crafts, and to possess them as handmaids.

paras.t: Timuerunt autem obstetrices Deum. Dicunt aliqui quod non solum servili, sed et filiali seu initiali timore Dominum timuerunt, ut infra tangetur. Et non fecerunt juxta præceptum regis Ægypti, sed conservabant, hoc est vivere permiserunt, mares, id est infantulos sexus masculini: nec etiam ceteris obstetricibus sibi subjectis commiserunt occidere masculos. Nec solum ex Dei timore, sed item ex naturali pietate et pia compassione abstinuerunt a tam crudelissima cæde, præsertim quum feminæ sint communiter ac naturaliter compassivæ ac molles.
paras.en: [[1:17|But the midwives feared God|Timuerunt autem obstetrices Deum]]. Some say that they feared the Lord not only with servile fear but also with filial or initial fear [servile fear dreads punishment; filial fear dreads offending God out of love; initial fear is the beginning of charity, between the two], as will be touched on below. [[1:17|and did not do as the king of Egypt had commanded, but saved|Et non fecerunt juxta præceptum regis Ægypti, sed conservabant]], that is, let live, [[1:17|the men children|mares]], that is, the little ones of the male sex; nor did they charge the other midwives under them to kill the males. And not only from the fear of God, but also from natural kindness and loving compassion, they held back from so very cruel a slaughter, especially since women are commonly and by nature compassionate and tender.

paras.t: Quibus ad se accersitis, rex ait. Quum enim rex percepisset per quosdam Ægyptios æmulos Hebræorum, quod obstetrices non interfecerunt masculos, vocavit rex eas ad se, dicens: Quidnam est hoc quod facere voluistis, ut pueros, scilicet masculos, servaretis? quasi dicat: Cur tam inobedientes mihi fuistis? Quæ responderunt: Non sunt Hebræ, sicut Ægyptiæ mulieres, id est, non sunt ita imperitæ in arte obstetricandi, ut Ægyptiæ feminæ. Ideo subditur: Ipsæ enim obstetricandi habent scientiam, et priusquam veniamus ad eas nos et obstetrices nobis subjectæ, pariunt, ita quod una earum alteri suffragatur, vel juvant se ipsas.
paras.en: [[1:18|And the king called for them and said|Quibus ad se accersitis, rex ait]]. For when the king had learned through certain Egyptians who were jealous of the Hebrews that the midwives had not killed the males, the king called them to him, saying: [[1:18|What is it that you meant to do|Quidnam est hoc quod facere voluistis]], [[1:18|that you would save the men children?|ut pueros, scilicet masculos, servaretis?]] [Denis adds *scilicet masculos*, "that is, the males", after *pueros*, "children"] as if to say: Why have you been so disobedient to me? [[1:19|They answered: The Hebrew women are not as the Egyptian women|Quæ responderunt: Non sunt Hebræ, sicut Ægyptiæ mulieres]], that is, they are not so unskilled in the art of midwifery as the Egyptian women. So there follows: [[1:19|for they themselves are skilful in the office of a midwife|Ipsæ enim obstetricandi habent scientiam]]; and [[1:19|before we come to them|priusquam veniamus ad eas]], we and the midwives under us, [[1:19|they are delivered|pariunt]], since one of them helps another, or they help themselves.

paras.t: Bene ergo fecit Deus obstetricibus, id est, earum pietatem ac timorem quo Deum timebant, et regem sceleratum offendere, seque periculo exponere maluerunt, quam tam dire peccare, remuneravit etiam in præsenti, ut paulo post diffusius exponetur. Et crevit populus Israel in sexu utroque, confortatusque est nimis. Et quia timuerunt obstetrices Deum, ædificavit illis domos. Hoc in Scholastica historia ita exponitur: Locupletavit eas, quum essent pauperes: vel fecundavit, quum essent steriles. Qui autem dicunt eas timuisse Deum filiali, vel saltem initiali timore, exponunt sic: Ædificavit eis domos, hoc est, spiritualem opulentiam gratiæ in præsenti contulit eis, mansiones quoque in gloria æternali eis paravit. Qui vero dicunt eas timuisse Deum timore solum servili, exponunt quod Deus ædificavit eis domos, id est, temporalia bona tribuit eis.
paras.en: [[1:20|Therefore God dealt well with the midwives|Bene ergo fecit Deus obstetricibus]], that is, he rewarded even in this present life their kindness and the fear with which they feared God and chose rather to offend a wicked king and put themselves in danger than to sin so dreadfully, as will be explained more fully a little later. [[1:20|and the people multiplied|Et crevit populus]] of Israel, in both sexes, [[1:20|and grew exceedingly strong|confortatusque est nimis]]. [[1:21|And because the midwives feared God, he built them houses|Et quia timuerunt obstetrices Deum, ædificavit illis domos]]. This is explained thus in the Scholastic History: He enriched them, when they were poor; or made them fruitful, when they were barren. Those who say that they feared God with filial, or at least initial, fear explain it thus: [[1:21|he built them houses|Ædificavit eis domos]], that is, he gave them in this present life the spiritual riches of grace, and also prepared them dwellings in eternal glory. But those who say that they feared God with servile fear only explain that God built them houses, that is, gave them temporal goods.

paras.t: Circa hoc quæritur, quali timore timuerunt Deum, et an peccaverint mortaliter se mendaciter excusando timore mortis, et amore vitæ præsentis, et utrum finaliter sint salvatæ. Ad ista S. Hieronymus super Isaiam innuit responsionem, dicendo quod Deus ædificavit eis domos, hoc est virtutes pro quibus in cœlestibus requiescerent. Ex quo sequitur, quod filiali aut initiali timore formidaverint Dominum, et venialiter tantum peccaverint mentiendo, quia mendacium illud fuit officiosum, non perniciosum, aut contra fidei veritatem, nec contra religionis doctrinam: et ita habuerunt virtutes infusas, et salvatæ creduntur. Idem sentit B. Augustinus, qui ait, et habetur in Glossa: Aliud faciebant obstetrices parvulos conservando, aliud Pharaoni mentiendo. In conservando opus misericordiæ fuit, mendacio autem pro se utebantur, ne Pharao eis noceret. Quod potuit non ad laudem, sed ad veniam pertinere: sicque earum mendacium exstitit veniale.
paras.en: On this it is asked with what fear they feared God, and whether they sinned mortally in excusing themselves with a lie, out of fear of death and love of this present life, and whether in the end they were saved. To these questions St. Jerome, on Isaias, points to an answer when he says that God built them houses, that is, virtues for which they might rest in heaven. From this it follows that they dreaded the Lord with filial or initial fear, and sinned only venially by lying, because that lie was officious [that is, a lie told to help someone or avert harm], not pernicious [that is, one that does harm], nor against the truth of the faith or the teaching of religion; and so they had the infused virtues and are believed to have been saved. Blessed Augustine thinks the same, who says (and it is in the Gloss): The midwives did one thing in saving the little ones, another in lying to Pharao. In saving them there was a work of mercy; but they used the lie for their own sake, so that Pharao should not harm them. This could belong not to praise, but to pardon; and so their lie was venial.

paras.t: Porro S. Gregorius sentire videtur, quod demerito sui mendacii, privatæ sunt retributione felicitatis æternæ, et sola temporalia pro præmio sunt sortitæ; quia per domos intelligit temporalia bona: sicque earum mendacium fuisset mortale. Hinc ex Gregorio fertur in Glossa: Summo opere cavendum est mendacium, quamvis sit culpæ levioris, si quis mentiatur præstando beneficium. Sed quoniam scriptum est, Os quod mentitur, occidit animam, hoc quoque perfecti refugiunt, ita ut nec vita cujuslibet per eorum fallaciam defendatur, ne noceant animæ suæ, dum prodesse cupiunt carni alienæ: quanquam hoc peccati genus facile relaxari credamus. Nam si quævis culpa sequenti pia operatione purgatur, quanto magis hæc facile abstergitur, quam mater boni operis pietas comitatur? Multi vero ex obstetricum fallacia conantur asserere, hoc mendacii genus non esse peccatum, quia ædificavit eis Dominus domos: in qua recompensatione magis agnoscitur, quid mendacii culpa mereatur. Nam benignitatis earum merces, quæ potuit in æterna vita retribui, in terrenam compensationem pro culpa mendacii est mutata, ut in vita sua, quam mentiendo tueri voluerunt, reciperent bona quæ fecerunt, et ulterius quod exspectarent mercedis præmium, non haberent. Nam et si subtiliter perpendatur, amore vitæ præsentis mentitæ sunt, non intentione mercedis. Parcendo enim, conatæ sunt infantum protegere vitam: mentiendo, suam.
paras.en: St. Gregory, however, seems to hold that by the demerit of their lie they were deprived of the reward of eternal happiness and received only temporal things as their reward, since by "houses" he understands temporal goods; and so their lie would have been mortal. Hence the Gloss gives from Gregory: A lie is to be avoided with the greatest care, even though the fault is lighter if one lies in doing a kindness. But since it is written, [[Wis 1:11|the mouth that belieth, killeth the soul|Os quod mentitur, occidit animam]], the perfect shun even this, so that not even anyone's life is defended by their deceit, lest they harm their own soul while they wish to help another's flesh; although we believe that this kind of sin is easily forgiven. For if any fault is cleansed by a good work that follows, how much more easily is this one wiped away, which is accompanied by kindness, the mother of good works? Many, however, try to argue from the deceit of the midwives that this kind of lie is no sin, because the Lord built them houses. But in that recompense it is rather seen what the fault of lying deserves. For the reward of their kindness, which could have been repaid in eternal life, was changed, because of the fault of lying, into an earthly recompense, so that in their life, which they had wished to protect by lying, they should receive the good they had done, and should have no further reward of wages to look for. For if it is weighed closely, they lied out of love of this present life, not with a view to reward: by sparing the infants they strove to protect their life; by lying, their own.

paras.t: Præterea, in his verbis videtur quædam contradictio insinuari. Si enim mendacium obstetricum fuit de facili relaxabile, faciliterque delebile, non videtur fuisse mortale: et si non fuit mortale, non propter illud sunt mercede cœlesti privatæ: nisi forte voluerit dicere, quod fuit faciliter delebile comparative loquendo, et ex causa seu ratione suæ originis. Denique non sequitur, mentitæ sunt amore vitæ præsentis, ergo sic mentiendo peccaverunt mortaliter. Non enim omne peccatum exstat mortale, quod oritur ex formidine mortis, aut amore vitæ præsentis: ut si quis evaginato gladio dicat alicui: Nisi protuleris mendacium jocosum aut officiosum, occidam te: et ille proferret tale mendacium, ne occideretur. Sed tunc est mortale, quod ex amore vitæ præsentis, aut mortis timore procedit, quando est contra præceptum aut caritatem. Tunc enim, et non aliter, vita præsens et amor ejus præferuntur caritati et vitæ æternæ, imo et Deo. Porro verba Gregorii quidam sic glossant: Si non essent mentitæ, Deus dedisset eis gratiam, per quam meruissent vitam æternam: sed mendacium earum fuit impedimentum infusionis gratiæ gratum facientis. Adduntque isti, quod obstetrices nunquam gratiam habuerunt: quod incertum opinor. Nec verum censetur, quod solum veniale peccatum impedivit eas a gratiæ infusione. Tamen si mori maluissent, quam mentiri ne Deum offenderent, gratiam utique seu ejus incrementum promeruissent.
paras.en: Moreover, a certain contradiction seems to be implied in these words. For if the midwives' lie was easily forgiven and easily blotted out, it seems not to have been mortal; and if it was not mortal, they were not deprived of the heavenly reward because of it: unless perhaps he meant that it was easily blotted out comparatively speaking, and by reason of the cause or nature of its origin. Again, it does not follow: they lied out of love of this present life, therefore by lying so they sinned mortally. For not every sin that springs from fear of death or love of this present life is mortal: as if someone with a drawn sword should say to another, Unless you tell a jocose or officious lie [a jocose lie is one told in jest], I will kill you, and he told such a lie so as not to be killed. But a sin that proceeds from love of this present life or fear of death is mortal when it is against a commandment or against charity. For then, and not otherwise, this present life and the love of it are preferred to charity and to eternal life, and indeed to God. Further, some gloss Gregory's words thus: If they had not lied, God would have given them grace, by which they would have merited eternal life; but their lie was a hindrance to the infusion of sanctifying grace [*gratia gratum faciens*, the grace that makes the soul pleasing to God]. And these add that the midwives never had grace, which I think uncertain. Nor is it thought true that a merely venial sin hindered them from the infusion of grace. Yet if they had chosen to die rather than lie, so as not to offend God, they would certainly have merited grace or its increase.

paras.t: Est ergo dicendum, quod mendacium obstetricum fuit veniale peccatum. Unde quod dicitur Deus eis domos ædificasse, exponi potest de retributione temporali ac spirituali. Nam et temporalium sufficientiam, et gratiam ac virtutes contulit illis, pro earum caritate et pietate ad Israelitas, proque timore quo Deum extimuerunt.
paras.en: It must be said, then, that the midwives' lie was a venial sin. Hence what is said, that God built them houses, can be explained of a temporal and a spiritual reward. For he gave them both a sufficiency of temporal things and grace and virtues, for their charity and kindness towards the Israelites, and for the fear with which they feared God.

paras.t: Creduntur quippe hæ obstetrices fuisse primo Ægyptiæ, sed Deo illuminante, acceperunt veri Dei notitiam. Et quamvis Pharao iste legatur ignorasse Joseph et ejus historiam, Israelitarumque Deum, non tamen est verisimile quin adhuc multi valde in Ægypto erant, qui ex revelatione aut conscriptione noverant inde loqui: inter quos forsitan erant et hæ obstetrices, quæ etiam inter Hebræos versando, aliquid discere potuerunt de vero Deo. Deinde per præfatam suam pietatem et compassionem, adeptæ creduntur gratiam tantam, quod ad cultum unius Dei conversæ sunt, ac promotæ in populo Hebræorum, sicut de Rahab legitur Josue sexto, et de Achior Ammonita in libro Judith. Nempe si Rahab consecuta est a Domino tantam remunerationem in bonis vitæ præsentis, atque in spiritualibus donis, quoniam duos Hebræorum exploratores pie tractavit, et a mortis discrimine liberavit: quanto magis obstetrices istæ, quæ circa tam multos innocentes infantulos, et per consequens circa eorum parentes fuerunt tam piæ ac gratiosæ? Quod autem per ædificationem domorum a Deo collatam obstetricibus illis, intelligi queant etiam facultates rei familiaris, seu bona terrena, testatur in libro de Locutionibus Augustinus.
paras.en: For these midwives are believed to have been Egyptians at first, but by God's enlightening they received the knowledge of the true God. And although this Pharao is read not to have known Joseph and his history, nor the God of the Israelites, yet it is not likely that there were not still very many in Egypt who, from revelation or from writings, knew how to speak of these things; and among them perhaps were these midwives too, who, moving among the Hebrews, could also learn something of the true God. Then, through their kindness and compassion already spoken of, they are believed to have obtained so great a grace that they were converted to the worship of the one God and advanced among the people of the Hebrews, as is read of Rahab in the sixth chapter of Josue[[Jos 6:25||]], and of Achior the Ammonite in the book of Judith[[Jdt 6:17||]][[Jdt 6:18||]]. Indeed, if Rahab obtained from the Lord so great a reward in the goods of this present life and in spiritual gifts because she dealt kindly with two spies of the Hebrews and delivered them from the danger of death, how much more these midwives, who were so kind and gracious towards so many innocent little ones, and consequently towards their parents? And that by the building of houses which God bestowed on those midwives household means, or earthly goods, can also be understood, Augustine testifies in the book of Locutions [his *Locutions on the Heptateuch*].

paras.t: Præcepit ergo Pharao omni populo suo, dicens: Quidquid masculini sexus natum fuerit ex Hebræis, in flumen, id est in Nilum, qui per diversa loca divisus, currit hinc inde per varias partes Ægypti, projicite: quidquid feminini, reservate. Itaque Pharao videns se non obtinere intentum per fraudes, et per persecutiones dolosas, in apertam persecutionem erupit. Erat autem projectio parvulorum in Nilum, minus horrenda, quam effusio sanguinis eorumdem: ideo magis præcepit rex ut mergerentur, quam ut ferro trucidarentur vel jugularentur. Quod vero legitur Pharao præcepisse istud omni populo suo, quidam de Ægyptiis interpretantur, ita quod illis jussit exsequi hoc mandatum, et inquirere diligenter, ubi, quando, et quid feminæ gignerent Hebræorum. Alii putant intelligendum de populo Israel, qui populus Pharaonis vocatur, quia sub ejus erat dominio. Unde et infra dicunt Hebræi ad Pharaonem: Cur ita agis contra populum tuum? Hi itaque dicunt, quod Pharao sub pœna mortis et amissionis rerum omnium, jussit viris Hebræis submergere proprios parvulos.
paras.en: [[1:22|Pharao therefore charged all his people, saying: Whatsoever shall be born of the male sex|Præcepit ergo Pharao omni populo suo, dicens: Quidquid masculini sexus natum fuerit]], of the Hebrews, [[1:22|into the river|in flumen]], that is, into the Nile, which, divided in various places, runs here and there through the different parts of Egypt, [[1:22|ye shall cast|projicite]]: [[1:22|whatsoever of the female, ye shall save alive|quidquid feminini, reservate]]. So Pharao, seeing that he was not getting his way by frauds and crafty persecutions, broke out into open persecution. Now the casting of the little ones into the Nile was less horrible than the shedding of their blood; so the king commanded rather that they be drowned than that they be slain or have their throats cut with the sword. That Pharao is read to have commanded this to all his people, some interpret of the Egyptians: that he ordered them to carry out this command, and to inquire diligently where, when and what the Hebrew women bore. Others think it is to be understood of the people of Israel, who are called Pharao's people because they were under his dominion. Hence below too the Hebrews say to Pharao: [[Ex 5:15|Why dealest thou so|Cur ita agis]] against thy people? [Denis reads *contra populum tuum*, "against thy people", where the Vulgate has *contra servos tuos*, "against thy servants"] These, then, say that Pharao, under pain of death and the loss of all their goods, ordered the Hebrew men to drown their own little ones.

paras.t: Amplius, præter rationem superius introductam, assignat Josephus aliam causam, cur Pharao jussit masculos, non femellas, occidi: videlicet quoniam quidam sacerdos Ægyptiorum prædixit regi, eo tempore masculum in Israel nasciturum, qui regimen Ægypti humiliaret, et virtute transcenderet universos. Istud quoque allegat Magister in historiis; imo S. Bernardus in sermone de Pascha circa epistolam sancti Joannis testatur, quod Herodes laborabat simili suspicione cum Pharaone: quoniam sicut Pharao præcepit universitatem parvulorum Israelitici germinis trucidari propter unum puerum sibi suspectum, ita Herodes parvulos Bethlehemitas. Sicque in hoc Moyses fuit figura Christi.
paras.en: Further, besides the reason given above, Josephus assigns another cause why Pharao ordered the males, not the females, to be killed: namely, because a certain priest of the Egyptians had foretold to the king that at that time a male would be born in Israel who would bring low the rule of Egypt and surpass all in virtue. The Master of the Histories also cites this; indeed St. Bernard, in a sermon for Easter on the epistle of St. John, testifies that Herod laboured under a suspicion like Pharao's: for as Pharao commanded the whole multitude of the little ones of the stock of Israel to be slain for the sake of one boy whom he suspected, so did Herod with the little ones of Bethlehem[[Matt 2:16||]]. And so in this Moses was a figure of Christ.

paras.t: Circa præhabita quæritur: An duæ præfatæ obstetrices Hebræorum, fuerunt natione Ægyptiæ, an Hebræ. Quocirca recitat Lyra: Dicunt Hebræi, quod fuerunt ambæ Hebræ, atque binomiæ, ita quod illa quæ in textu vocatur Sephora, fuit Jochabed filia Levi, et secunda Maria soror Moysis. Quod improbat Lyra: Primo, quoniam Jochabed illa jam mortua fuit, quum dictum sit, quod Joseph et fratres ejus omnisque cognatio illa jam erant defuncti. Secundo, quoniam obstetrices illæ excusando se coram rege, dixerunt: Non sunt Hebrææ, sicut Ægyptiæ mulieres. Per quod insinuari videtur, quod ipsæ non erant Hebrææ. Tertio, quoniam non est probabile, quod occultam interfectionem infantium Hebræorum commisit rex mulieribus Hebræis. His addi potest, quod Jochabed etsi adhuc vixisset, tamen præ nimia senectute inepta fuisset ad obstetricale officium ac generalem sollicitudinem obstetricum. Maria vero soror Moysis, fuit puella tam juvenis, quod tunc fuisset ad officium illud inepta. Vix enim erat quindecim annorum. Josephus quoque ait, quod erant Ægyptiæ, et quod propter hoc rex putavit eas suam non transgredi jussionem.
paras.en: On what has been said it is asked whether the two midwives of the Hebrews spoken of were Egyptians or Hebrews by nation. On this Lyra reports: The Hebrews say that both were Hebrews, and had two names, so that the one called Sephora in the text was Jochabed, the daughter of Levi, and the second was Mary, the sister of Moses. Lyra disproves this: first, because that Jochabed was already dead, since it has been said that Joseph and his brethren and all that generation were already dead[[1:6||]]. Secondly, because those midwives, excusing themselves before the king, said: [[1:19|The Hebrew women are not as the Egyptian women|Non sunt Hebrææ, sicut Ægyptiæ mulieres]]; by which it seems to be implied that they themselves were not Hebrews. Thirdly, because it is not probable that the king entrusted the secret killing of the Hebrews' infants to Hebrew women. To these it can be added that Jochabed, even had she still been alive, would have been unfit, by reason of her great age, for the office of midwife and for the general oversight of the midwives; while Mary, the sister of Moses, was then so young a girl that she would have been unfit for that office, for she was hardly fifteen years old. Josephus too says that they were Egyptians, and that for this reason the king thought they would not transgress his command.

1.title: Expositio spiritualis ejusdem primi capituli
1.title_en: Spiritual exposition of the same first chapter

paras.t: Secundum Origenem, sermo sacræ Scripturæ similis est semini in terram projecto, quod crescit in plurima grana: et tanto fructuosius redditur, quanto ab agricola fuerit diligentius cultum, et quo terra pinguior uberiorque exstiterit. Sic una scriptura multipliciorem parit sensum, et tanto salubriores gignit sententias, quanto profundius consideratur, et quo cor considerantis, sicut adipe et pinguedine, amplius adimpletur dono sapientiæ et spiritu intellectus. Ita est plane de hoc in Exodo. Quod, quantum ad superficiem litteræ, exstat perfacile; sed spiritualiter ac mystice consideratum, sensus habet sublimes.
paras.en: According to Origen, the word of sacred Scripture is like seed cast into the ground, which grows into a great many grains: and it yields the more fruit the more diligently it has been tended by the farmer, and the richer and more fertile the soil has been. So one passage of Scripture brings forth a manifold sense, and gives rise to the more wholesome teachings the more deeply it is considered, and the more the heart of him who considers it is filled, [[Ps 62:6|as with marrow and fatness|sicut adipe et pinguedine]], with the gift of wisdom and the spirit of understanding. So it plainly is with this passage of Exodus. As to the surface of the letter it is very easy; but considered spiritually and mystically, it holds sublime senses.

paras.t: Itaque per ingressum Jacob et undecim filiorum ejus cum eorum familiis in Ægyptum ut ibi reficerentur, mystice designatur, quod Dominus noster Jesus Christus per Jacob præfiguratus, intravit hunc mundum desiderio nostræ salutis, et cum ipso undecim Apostoli præelecti, quorum duodecimus fuit reprobus et iniquus, sicut de ipso asseruit Christus: Unus ex vobis diabolus est. Deinde Judæa relicta, Christus in Apostolis et per eos regna gentilium est ingressus. Porro, per familias Patriarcharum, intelliguntur spirituales filii Apostolorum, quos sancti Apostoli assumpserunt in adjutorium, atque miserunt ad gentium conversionem. Per animas quoque septuaginta, seu septuaginta quinque, intelliguntur septuaginta discipuli Christi, qui ante vixerunt juxta legem ac documenta quinque librorum Moysis. Per hoc quoque, quod Joseph tunc exstitit in Ægypto quando undecim Patriarchæ erant cum Jacob, datur intelligi, quod Paulus nondum conversus, adhuc inter mundanos conversabatur, quando undecim Apostoli erant cum Christo, Juda sublato. Verumtamen per hoc aptius designatur, quod Christus secundum suæ deitatis incircumscriptibilem majestatem fuit ubique terrarum, quando secundum suam humanitatem fuit et ambulavit cum Apostolis in loco determinato. Propter quod ait Evangelista de Christo: In mundo erat, et mundus per ipsum factus est. Et nunc nondum cognoverat eum mundus, sed ut cognosceretur, venit per Apostolos ad mundanos. Christus equidem qui designatur per Jacob, significatur et per Joseph: quum tanta sit perfectio et abundantia mysteriorum Christi, quod per unum, imo per plures non potest plenarie præfigurari.
paras.en: So by the entry of Jacob and his eleven sons with their households into Egypt, that they might be fed there, it is mystically signified that our Lord Jesus Christ, prefigured by Jacob, entered this world out of desire for our salvation, and with Him the eleven Apostles chosen beforehand, the twelfth of whom was reprobate and wicked, as Christ declared of him: [[John 6:71|one of you is a devil|Unus ex vobis diabolus est]]. Then, leaving Judea, Christ in the Apostles and through them entered the kingdoms of the gentiles. Further, by the households of the Patriarchs are understood the spiritual sons of the Apostles, whom the holy Apostles took to help them and sent out to convert the gentiles. By the seventy souls also, or seventy-five [that is, the number given in Acts 7:14], are understood the seventy disciples of Christ, who had lived before according to the law and teachings of the five books of Moses. By this too, that Joseph was then in Egypt when the eleven Patriarchs were with Jacob, we are given to understand that Paul, not yet converted, was still living among worldly men when the eleven Apostles were with Christ, Judas having been taken away. Yet what is more fittingly signified by this is that Christ, according to the uncircumscribable majesty of His Godhead, was everywhere on earth, while according to His humanity He was, and walked with the Apostles, in a determined place. For this reason the Evangelist says of Christ: [[John 1:10|He was in the world: and the world was made by him|In mundo erat, et mundus per ipsum factus est]]. And as yet the world had not known Him, but that He might be known, He came through the Apostles to worldly men. Indeed Christ, who is signified by Jacob, is signified also by Joseph: since the perfection and abundance of the mysteries of Christ is so great that it cannot be fully prefigured by one, nay, not even by several.

paras.t: Quo mortuo, et universis fratribus ejus, omnique cognatione illa, filii Israel creverunt, et quasi germinantes multiplicati sunt; ac roborati nimis, impleverunt terram. Sic Domino Jesu Christo crucifixo ac mortuo, sanctis quoque Apostolis ac primis discipulis in fide et pro fide Christi martyrizatis, Christiani qui sunt veri ac spirituales Israelitæ, ubique terrarum super arenam sunt multiplicati, suisque hostibus tam invisibilibus quam visibilibus per fidem et patientiam, per caritatis fervorem, fortitudinisque constantiam ac virtutem prævaluerunt. Nam tempore persecutionum et tyrannorum magis excrevit Ecclesia, imo sæpissime in martyrizatione unius Sancti aut Sanctæ, omnipotens Deus tot et tanta peregit miracula, quod ad Christum convertebantur gentilium millia multa, quemadmodum Christus ante suam passionem promisit atque prædixit discipulis: Ego, inquiens, dabo vobis os et sapientiam, cui non poterunt resistere et contradicere omnes adversarii vestri.
paras.en: [[1:6|After he was dead, and all his brethren, and all that generation|Quo mortuo, et universis fratribus ejus, omnique cognatione illa]], [[1:7|The children of Israel increased, and sprung up into multitudes, and growing exceedingly strong they filled the land|filii Israel creverunt, et quasi germinantes multiplicati sunt; ac roborati nimis, impleverunt terram]]. So, when the Lord Jesus Christ had been crucified and had died, and the holy Apostles too and the first disciples had been martyred in the faith and for the faith of Christ, the Christians, who are the true and spiritual Israelites, were multiplied over all the earth beyond the sand, and prevailed over their enemies, invisible as well as visible, by faith and patience, by the fervour of charity, and by the constancy and virtue of fortitude. For in the time of persecutions and tyrants the Church grew the more; nay, very often at the martyrdom of a single saint, man or woman, almighty God worked so many and such great miracles that many thousands of the gentiles were converted to Christ, as Christ before His passion promised and foretold to the disciples, saying: [[Luke 21:15|I|Ego]], He says, [[Luke 21:15|will give you a mouth and wisdom, which all your adversaries shall not be able to resist and gainsay|dabo vobis os et sapientiam, cui non poterunt resistere et contradicere omnes adversarii vestri]].

paras.t: Insuper, juxta tropologicum sensum, mortuo Joseph, hoc est, homine christiano per Christi cruciformem imitationem salubriter mortificato ac reformato, crescunt in eo filii Israel, hoc est sensus spirituales ac mystici virtuosique actus, et contemplationum excessus, ita ut revelata facie gloriam Domini speculetur, et membra corporis sui fructificent Deo, quoniam exhibentur arma justitiæ Regi æterno. Talisque homo oratione, prædicatione, exemplari quoque conversatione multos convertit, ac generat Domino.
paras.en: Moreover, in the tropological sense [that is, the moral sense, concerning the soul], when Joseph is dead, that is, when the Christian man has been wholesomely mortified and reformed by imitating Christ in the form of the cross, the children of Israel grow in him, that is, spiritual and mystical understandings, virtuous acts, and ecstasies of contemplation, so that he is [[2 Cor 3:18|beholding the glory of the Lord with open face|revelata facie gloriam Domini speculetur]], and the members of his body bear fruit to God, since they are yielded as instruments of justice to the eternal King. And such a man, by prayer, by preaching and by the example of his life, converts many and begets them to the Lord.

paras.t: Surrexit interea rex novus super Ægyptum, etc. Per novum regem illum, ingratum Christo et ejus ignarum, intelligitur unusquisque tyrannus, qui videns Christianos multiplicatos ac roboratos, tractat cum subditis suis, qualiter Christianos queat opprimere, et nomen Christi delere de terra, quoniam videt se sapientiæ Christianorum non posse resistere. Hoc primo fecerunt indurati pontifices Judæorum, persequendo atrociter primitivam Ecclesiam, deinde reges et principes paganorum, præsertim imperatores Romanorum atque Persarum. Primusque Nero generalem concitavit persecutionem in Christianos. Diocletianus vero et Maximianus ferventissime affectabant ac laborabant, universam plebem christifidelem ejusque memoriam et nomen Christi prorsus auferre de terra.
paras.en: [[1:8|In the mean time there arose a new king over Egypt|Surrexit interea rex novus super Ægyptum]], etc. By that new king, unfriendly to Christ and ignorant of Him, is understood every tyrant who, seeing the Christians multiplied and strengthened, takes counsel with his subjects how he may oppress the Christians and blot out the name of Christ from the earth, since he sees that he cannot resist the wisdom of the Christians. This the hardened high priests of the Jews did first, cruelly persecuting the primitive Church; then the kings and princes of the pagans, above all the emperors of the Romans and of the Persians. Nero was the first to stir up a general persecution against the Christians. Diocletian and Maximian strove and laboured most ardently to take away from the earth altogether the whole Christian people, its memory, and the name of Christ.

paras.t: Præposuit itaque eis magistros operum, etc. Hoc totum etiam quasi ad litteram impletum est in populo christiano. Quemadmodum enim Pharao præposuit filiis Israel magistros operum, ut affligerent eos oneribus, sic multi reges principesque pagani injunxerunt Christianis labores gravissimos, ut scilicet metalla effoderent, lutum et saxa portarent, ac tributa persolverent. Præterea, quanto plus opprimebantur fideles per martyria et labores, tanto amplius merito ac numero aucti sunt. Ideo oderunt eos Ægyptii, puta increduli, qui illuserunt et afflixerunt credentes in Christum, atque ad amaritudinem corporalium pœnarum perducebant vitam fidelium, per opera dura luti ac lateris, utpote per labores et servitutes gravissimas in rebus vilibus ac terrenis, quamvis sancti Christiani omnia talia propter Christum æquanimiter ferrent in spiritu.
paras.en: [[1:11|Therefore he set over them masters of the works|Præposuit itaque eis magistros operum]], etc. All this too was fulfilled almost to the letter in the Christian people. For as Pharao set masters of the works over the children of Israel to afflict them with burdens, so many pagan kings and princes laid the heaviest labours on the Christians: to dig out metals, that is, to carry clay and stones, and to pay tributes. Moreover, the more the faithful were oppressed by martyrdoms and labours, the more they increased in merit and in number. Therefore the Egyptians hated them, that is, the unbelievers, who mocked and afflicted those who believed in Christ, and made the life of the faithful bitter with bodily punishments, by hard works of clay and brick, that is, by the heaviest labours and servitude in base and earthly things, although the holy Christians bore all such things for Christ's sake with an even mind in the spirit.

paras.t: Per reges demum Ægypti, qui noverant Joseph et beneficia ejus, nec filiis Israel molesti fuerunt, signantur principes christiani, sub quibus Ecclesia pacem temporis ac pectoris est sortita.
paras.en: Lastly, by the kings of Egypt who knew Joseph and his benefits and did not trouble the children of Israel, are signified the Christian princes, under whom the Church obtained peace both of the times and of the heart.

paras.t: Insuper, per regem Ægypti afflictorem Israelitarum, significatur diabolus, qui dum primitivam Ecclesiam vidisset quotidie mirabiliter multiplicari, omnique divinorum charismatum virtute ac gratia roborari et expoliri, dixit satellitibus suis: Ecce populus filiorum Israel, id est Christianorum, qui per fidei imitationem sunt filii Abrahæ, et per contemplationem divinorum digni sunt Israel appellari; multus, et fortior nobis est: quia per opem Spiritus Sancti prævaluerunt dæmonibus, ejeceruntque eos ab obsessis, et de cordibus horum quos converterunt. Hinc ait Salvator discipulis: Ecce dedi vobis potestatem calcandi super serpentes et scorpiones, et supra omnem virtutem inimici. Venite, sapienter opprimamus eum, id est pondere tentationum et impetu adversitatum: dæmones autem suam nequissimam calliditatem, sapientiam arbitrantur: ne forte multiplicetur in personis et meritis: et si ingruerit contra nos bellum, hoc est, si alii quoque adhuc infideles receperint fidem, seque opposuerint nobis, addatur inimicis nostris, id est, caritative ac pie se applicet illis recenter conversis: expugnatisque nobis, egrediatur de terra, hoc est de exsilio suæ peregrinationis et corpore mortis, seu terrena et carnalia vitia omnino relinquat, et intret in regnum cœleste.
paras.en: Further, by the king of Egypt who afflicted the Israelites is signified the devil, who, when he had seen the primitive Church wonderfully multiplied day by day, and strengthened and adorned with every power and grace of the divine charisms, said to his henchmen: [[1:9|Behold the people of the children of Israel|Ecce populus filiorum Israel]], that is, of the Christians, who by imitating his faith are sons of Abraham, and by the contemplation of divine things are worthy to be called Israel [that is, by the old etymology, “a man seeing God”]; [[1:9|are numerous and stronger than we|multus, et fortior nobis est]]: because by the help of the Holy Ghost they prevailed over the demons, and cast them out of the possessed, and out of the hearts of those whom they converted. Hence the Saviour says to the disciples: [[Luke 10:19|Behold, I have given you power to tread upon serpents and scorpions and upon all the power of the enemy|Ecce dedi vobis potestatem calcandi super serpentes et scorpiones, et supra omnem virtutem inimici]]. [[1:10|Come let us wisely oppress them|Venite, sapienter opprimamus eum]], that is, with the weight of temptations and the onset of adversities: for the demons take their most wicked cunning for wisdom: [[1:10|lest they multiply|ne forte multiplicetur]] in persons and in merits: [[1:10|and if any war shall rise against us|et si ingruerit contra nos bellum]], that is, if others too who are still unbelievers receive the faith and set themselves against us, [[1:10|join with our enemies|addatur inimicis nostris]], that is, attach themselves in charity and devotion to those newly converted: [[1:10|and having overcome us, depart out of the land|expugnatisque nobis, egrediatur de terra]], that is, out of the exile of their pilgrimage and the body of death, or leave earthly and carnal vices altogether, and enter into the kingdom of heaven.

paras.t: Præposuit itaque eis magistros operum, ut affligerent eos oneribus. Isti magistri operum, sunt maligni spiritus, ad certa distincta vitia inclinantes, ac variis modis tentantes genus humanum. Quibus præcipit princeps tenebrarum, ut affligant fideles per terrores et somnia, per tentationes et tribulationes multiplices. Hinc quidam dæmonum vocantur spiritus fornicationis, alii spiritus superbiæ, alii spiritus invidiæ, alii iræ, aliique acediæ. Ædificaveruntque urbes tabernaculorum Pharaoni. Hi etenim qui ad tempus credunt, et facta persecutione scandalizantur, ac tentatione vincuntur, ædificant urbes tabernaculorum Pharaonis, id est, congregationes faciunt pravas, in quibus regnat diabolus.
paras.en: [[1:11|Therefore he set over them masters of the works, to afflict them with burdens|Præposuit itaque eis magistros operum, ut affligerent eos oneribus]]. These masters of the works are the evil spirits, which incline to certain particular vices and tempt mankind in various ways. The prince of darkness commands them to afflict the faithful with terrors and dreams, with temptations and manifold tribulations. Hence some of the demons are called spirits of fornication, others spirits of pride, others spirits of envy, others of anger, and others of sloth [the Latin is acedia, the spiritual sloth that wearies of the things of God]. [[1:11|and they built for Pharao cities of tabernacles|Ædificaveruntque urbes tabernaculorum Pharaoni]]. For those who [[Luke 8:13|believe for a while|ad tempus credunt]], and are scandalized when persecution comes, and are overcome by temptation, build cities of tabernacles for Pharao, that is, they form wicked communities in which the devil reigns.

paras.t: Quantoque opprimebant eos, tanto magis multiplicabantur. Hoc impletur in his, qui radices cordis fixerunt in Deo, et timorati ac justi sunt: qui tanto ardentius atque intentius insistunt exercitiis virtuosis, et tentationibus renituntur, quanto acrius se tentari experiuntur, quemadmodum ad Hebræos hortatur Apostolus: Deponentes omne pondus et circumstans nos peccatum, per patientiam curramus ad propositum nobis certamen, adspicientes in auctorem fidei et consummatorem Jesum.
paras.en: [[1:12|But the more they oppressed them, the more they were multiplied|Quantoque opprimebant eos, tanto magis multiplicabantur]]. This is fulfilled in those who have fixed the roots of their heart in God, and are God-fearing and just: who apply themselves to virtuous exercises and resist temptations the more ardently and earnestly, the more sharply they find themselves tempted, as the Apostle exhorts the Hebrews: [[Heb 12:1|laying aside every weight and sin which surrounds us, let us run by patience to the fight proposed to us|Deponentes omne pondus et circumstans nos peccatum, per patientiam curramus ad propositum nobis certamen]], [[Heb 12:2|Looking on Jesus, the author and finisher of faith|adspicientes in auctorem fidei et consummatorem Jesum]] [the margin's chapter and verse are lost; the words are Heb 12:1–2].

paras.t: Oderantque filii Israel Ægyptii: id est, dæmones multipliciter odiunt Christianos, quos indesinenter conantur decipere. Nam et invidia diaboli, mors intravit in orbem terrarum. Et affligebant, illudentes eis. Utique invisibiles hostes per tentationes, distractiones, et varias phantasias ac persuasiones, quas ingerunt cordibus devotorum, valde affligunt eosdem, et frequenter eis illudunt, ita quod dum Deo cum sinceritate et fervore intenderent, atque stabiliter inhærerent, vanis ac frivolis imaginationibus occupantur, etiam tempore orationis ac cultus divini. Propter quod oravit Propheta: Deus meus, in te confido, non erubescam, neque irrideant me inimici mei.
paras.en: [[1:13|And the Egyptians hated the children of Israel|Oderantque filii Israel Ægyptii]]: that is, the demons hate the Christians in many ways, and ceaselessly try to deceive them. For [[Wis 2:24|by the envy of the devil, death came into the world|invidia diaboli, mors intravit in orbem terrarum]]. [[1:13|and afflicted them and mocked them|Et affligebant, illudentes eis]]. Indeed the invisible enemies, by temptations, distractions, and various fancies and persuasions which they thrust into the hearts of the devout, afflict them greatly and often mock them, so that while they would attend to God with sincerity and fervour and cleave to Him steadfastly, they are taken up with vain and frivolous imaginings, even in the time of prayer and divine worship. For this reason the Prophet prayed: [[Ps 24:2|In thee, O my God, I put my trust; let me not be ashamed|Deus meus, in te confido, non erubescam]], [[Ps 24:3|Neither let my enemies laugh at me|neque irrideant me inimici mei]] [the margin gives Ps. xxiv without a verse].

paras.t: Atque ad amaritudinem perducebant vitam eorum operibus duris luti et lateris. Electi interdum graviter amaricantur, dum eis a dæmonibus carnalia vitia suggeruntur, vel dum in ea corruisse se gemunt. Opera quippe luti ac lateris, recte dicuntur immundissimi actus luxuriæ, quæ maculat tanquam lutum; et pravæ consuetudinis, quæ instar lateris, intenso propriæ voluntatis affectu induruit. Unde Psalmista decantat: Exaudivit Dominus preces meas, et eduxit me de lacu miseriæ et de luto fæcis. Itaque ad hæc inquinamenta et consuetudinem pravam conantur spiritus maligni inducere homines.
paras.en: [[1:14|And they made their life bitter with hard works in clay and brick|Atque ad amaritudinem perducebant vitam eorum operibus duris luti et lateris]]. The elect are sometimes made grievously bitter when carnal vices are suggested to them by the demons, or when they groan at having fallen into them. For the works of clay and brick are rightly said to be the most unclean acts of lust, which stains like clay; and of evil habit, which, like brick, has hardened through the intense affection of one's own will. Hence the Psalmist sings of the Lord: [[Ps 39:3|he heard my prayers, and brought me out of the pit of misery and the mire of dregs|Exaudivit Dominus preces meas, et eduxit me de lacu miseriæ et de luto fæcis]] [the margin gives Ps. xxxix without a verse]. So it is to these defilements and to evil habit that the evil spirits try to draw men.

paras.t: Dixit autem rex Ægypti obstetricibus Hebræorum. Per obstetrices Hebræorum, intelliguntur animæ timoratorum præsidentium, quæ subditos quasi modo genitos infantes lacte spiritualis doctrinæ reficiunt. Talibus animabus diabolus suggerit, ut mares parvulos perimant, feminas reservent: id est, spirituales humilesque errare sinant ac perire, nec eos hortentur, consolentur, corripiant ac castigent: feminas vero, id est carnales et molles, in suis permittant carnalitatibus, negligentiis, ac perversitatibus perdurare et in talibus foveant eos.
paras.en: [[1:15|And the king of Egypt spoke to the midwives of the Hebrews|Dixit autem rex Ægypti obstetricibus Hebræorum]]. By the midwives of the Hebrews are understood the souls of God-fearing superiors, who feed their subjects, as newborn babes, with the milk of spiritual doctrine[[1 Pet 2:2||]] [the margin note here is unreadable; the words recall 1 Pet 2:2]. The devil suggests to such souls that they kill the little males and keep the females: that is, that they let the spiritual and humble go astray and perish, and do not exhort, console, rebuke and chastise them; but the females, that is, the carnal and soft, they are to let continue in their carnal ways, negligences and perversities, and to cherish them in such things.

paras.t: Huic tam impiæ suggestioni diaboli, non acquiescunt animæ prælatorum et doctorum Deum timentium. Quumque diabolus hoc ipsum eis improperat, dicunt: Non sunt Hebrææ, sicut Ægyptiæ mulieres, id est, animæ Christifidelium, non sunt sicut animæ infidelium ac pravorum. Ipsæ enim obstetricandi habent scientiam, hoc est, animæ veraciter christianæ, desuper illustratæ, ex unctione Spiritus Sancti agnoscunt, qualiter cogitationes et affectus in se omni hora nascentes, debeant dijudicare, discernere, dirigere, et mala cordis germina a se statim abjicere. Ideo priusquam veniamus ad eas, pariunt, id est, antequam informentur a nobis, ex illuminatione divina recte se habent, et fructum virtutis pariunt. Unde Joannes apostolus in prima sua Canonica talibus subditis scribit: Non necesse habetis ut aliquis doceat vos, sed unctio ejus docet vos de omnibus. Paulus quoque: Divites, inquit, facti estis in Deo, in omni verbo et scientia, ita ut non sit necesse nobis aliquid loqui.
paras.en: To this so impious suggestion of the devil the souls of prelates and teachers who fear God do not consent. And when the devil reproaches them for this very thing, they say: [[1:19|The Hebrew women are not as the Egyptian women|Non sunt Hebrææ, sicut Ægyptiæ mulieres]], that is, the souls of the faithful of Christ are not like the souls of unbelievers and the wicked. [[1:19|for they themselves are skilful in the office of a midwife|Ipsæ enim obstetricandi habent scientiam]], that is, truly Christian souls, enlightened from above, know by the unction of the Holy Ghost how they ought to judge, discern and direct the thoughts and affections that spring up in them at every hour, and to cast the evil shoots of the heart from them at once. Therefore [[1:19|they are delivered before we come to them|priusquam veniamus ad eas, pariunt]], that is, before they are instructed by us, they are rightly disposed through divine enlightenment, and bring forth the fruit of virtue. Hence John the Apostle writes to such subjects in his first Canonical Epistle: [[1 John 2:27|you have no need that any man teach you: but as his unction teacheth you of all things|Non necesse habetis ut aliquis doceat vos, sed unctio ejus docet vos de omnibus]]. Paul also: [[1 Cor 1:5|you are made rich|Divites]], he says, [[1 Cor 1:5|in him, in all utterance and in all knowledge|facti estis in Deo, in omni verbo et scientia]], [[1 Thess 1:8|so that we need not to speak any thing|ita ut non sit necesse nobis aliquid loqui]].

paras.t: Bene ergo fecit Deus obstetricibus; et ædificavit eis domos: id est, animabus talium prælatorum ac præsidentium, contulit Deus copiosissima munera gratiæ ac virtutum in vita præsenti, atque in cœlestibus mansionibus præparavit beatissimas sedes, ut non solum coronentur pro propriis meritis, sed item pro meritis omnium quos digne rexerunt. Sub talium autem regimine maxime crescit ac proficit populus christianus.
paras.en: [[1:20|Therefore God dealt well with the midwives|Bene ergo fecit Deus obstetricibus]]; [[1:21|he built them houses|et ædificavit eis domos]]: that is, on the souls of such prelates and superiors God bestowed most abundant gifts of grace and virtues in the present life, and prepared for them most blessed seats in the heavenly mansions, that they may be crowned not only for their own merits but also for the merits of all whom they have worthily ruled. And under the rule of such men the Christian people grows and advances most of all.

paras.t: Præcepit ergo Pharao omni populo suo, dicens: Quidquid masculini sexus natum fuerit, in flumen projicite; quidquid feminini, reservate. Populus Pharaonis sunt dæmones, principi suo subjecti; omnes quoque iniqui, hæretici, schismatici, infideles, quibus omnibus jubet ac suggerit diabolus, ut masculos in flumen projiciant, id est, vere catholicos, justos ac spirituales persequantur ac destruant, obruendo eosdem inquietudine tribulationum, impetu tentationum, fluxu et abundantia vitiorum: feminas autem reservent, id est, eos in malis foveant et conservent, qui instar feminarum instabiles sunt, molles ac debiles ad resistendum tentamentis ac vitiis.
